Gaming_Tech.title: Details of thousands of US immigration agents leaked in major hack
Gaming_Tech.text:
Details of more than 41,000 personnel working for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), including thousands involved in immigration enforcement, have been leaked to the public.

The leak includes names, work addresses and phone numbers of DHS staff, including agents working with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection, along with descriptions of the work they do for each agency.

Wednesday's leak marks the third time in recent weeks that a government agency has been targeted by leaks or hacks.

A DHS spokesperson said the agency is "aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively."

"We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected," the spokesperson added.

"We will update the public when more information is available."

The seemingly unprecedented breach of employee information was made public online. A group called the Department of Peace accessed the information from DHS, while journalist and cybersecurity researcher maia crimew alongside the website Distributed Denial of Secrets put it online.

The information was put in a database named Icepick.

Most of the agents included, more than 21,000 of them, work for CBP, according to the data. Nearly 6,600 work for ICE.

Other records show agents with Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Protective Service and even people working for the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

The leaked information also included dozens of previously unknown operation names, the agents that led and worked on those operations, and some of the technology they used in their work, including tech provided by Cellbrite and Palantir.

The groups wrote in an online statement that the the leak was not meant to be a directory of every DHS agent. Rather the aim was to replace "anonymity with accountability", according to Emma Best, a co founder of DDoSecrets.

"The leak is extraordinary but deceptive in its simplicity as it identifies the officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations, the government's hunt for leakers and the failed BlueLeaks investigation - along with key personnel in DHS's ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs," Best added.

BlueLeaks refers to a massive leak of US police data in 2020, data from which DDoSecrets also hosted.

A spokesperson for the Department of Peace pointed directly at actions by ICE agents for the group's work to hack DHS records.

"On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was 'turning up the heat'. This is what happens to ICE when you do that," the spokesperson wrote on Wednesday.

Mullin in March became Secretary of Homeland Security.

The Department of Peace said it accessed the DHS agent profiles through a single sign-on service called Okta.

Okta is a popular online security tool that organisations use to ensure that only people with access to internal platforms are logging on to them.

A spokeswoman for Okta said the company is aware of the claims being made, but said: "Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised."

Last month, the FBI was hacked by a group called ShinyHunters, which took personal information about thousands of agents.

In recent days, the Federal Election Commission, which makes public political campaign donation data, was taken offline because of a suspected hacking attempt.

Public backlash to US immigration enforcement has been building as the Trump Administration has pushed a huge increase in arrests and deportations of people suspected of being in the country illegally.

Immigration operations this year have repeatedly turned violent, external, with ICE agents shooting at more than two dozen people and killing at least nine people.

Those killings include the high profile deaths of Alex Pretti and Renee Good, both of whom were shot and killed by ICE agents this year in Minnesota, despite not being the targets of arrests.

Often, ICE agents carry out enforcement actions while their faces are covered by masks and sunglasses. Immigration agents rarely identify themselves, despite being required by law to do so, and US politicians have publicly demanded, external DHS enforces the requirement.

Gaming_Tech.title: Shop fridges and freezers across Europe hit by fresh suspected cyber-attack
Gaming_Tech.text:
Supermarket chains in at least seven European countries have said the temperatures of refrigerators and freezers in some of their shops soared overnight to as high as 50C (122F), echoing a cyber-attack last month that caused millions of euros of damage in France.

Retailers in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with their refrigeration systems on Monday, and several companies confirmed they had been hacked.

The EU food and agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, said the repeated cyber-attacks were deeply concerning, calling them “a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it”.

The incidents follow an attack in France last month in which hackers seized control of cooling units in as many as 700 supermarkets, raising their temperatures as high ⁠as 50C (122F) and causing fires and food losses estimated in the tens of millions of euros.

A growing range of devices, including refrigeration systems, can now be monitored and controlled remotely, leading authorities to particularly fear government-sponsored hybrid attacks ​in after Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

Sweden’s Coop chain told the daily Aftonbladet that six of ​its shops ‌had been ​hit, while ICA said it was “aware that a limited ​number of stores were affected by an incident overnight which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems”.

An ICA shop at Sjöbo in southern Sweden posted that its fridges and freezers had been hacked and their temperature set at 50C. Another in Stockholm said its freezers were broken “due to a 2am cyberattack” and that “everything was destroyed”.

The head of Sweden’s national cybersecurity centre, John Billow, said it ‌was working on incidents around the country. It had established the country had “quite a lot of exposed operational ‌technology devices” that needed updating or patching, he told Reuters.

The Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, which last ​month ​reported a ​similar incident ​to police in the Netherlands, said fridges and ⁠freezers in dozens of its ⁠supermarkets in ​Belgium ‌and ‌Luxembourg had been hit.

It did not specify the cause, but reporters visiting a shop north-east of Brussels saw refrigerators and freezers empty and a sign reading: “Due to cyberattacks, there will be no products on the refrigerated or freezer shelves. We offer our sincere apologies.”

A company spokesperson, Sarah ‌De Meester, said the range of fresh and frozen products was “temporarily somewhat limited” in affected shops, but that distribution centres were operating normally and there was no disruption to deliveries.

Belgium’s Le Soir newspaper reported that dozens of shops and supermarkets had been affected, including five Spar outlets, Shop & Go convenience shops attached to Q8 service stations and some smaller Proxy Delhaize mini-markets.

“We started mobilising technicians at 1am,” Stephan Moelans, the chief executive of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize’s refrigeration systems, told the paper. “We spent all night and morning disconnecting the affected installations.”

He told the Belga news agency the ‌incident had been a cyber-attack and that the units’ evaporators were switched to defrost mode.

The Colruyt and Intermarché supermarket chains also said they had been hit by technical problems affecting fridges in five and 15 of their shops respectively, and Carrefour Belgium reported disruption in about 15 of its 700 shops.

“It’s a cyber-attack, there is no other reason,” said Mich Vergauwen, a Carrefour spokesperson. An Ikea Belgium spokesperson likewise told Agence France-Presse that a cyber-attack had caused the temperature of freezers in its Mons shop to rise suddenly.

Ikea, famous for its in-store Swedish meatballs, said it had had to ‌remove some food products from refrigeration units ​as a precaution and expected some food waste as ⁠a result.

In Finland, the Helsingin Sanomat newspaper said shops operated by the Kesko supermarket chain were investigating similar problems, while the Dutch public radio NOS reported that the systems of at least 17 mainly small local shops had been affected.

At one Estonian supermarket chain, attackers accessed a computer controlling the refrigeration system and turned up the temperature to 50C, the refrigeration supply company Kitman Coldtech told the ERR broadcaster.

“This is very fresh, it happened this morning,” its chief executive, Jann Mutso, said, adding that the attack was responded to within minutes and there had been no significant damage. The Selver supermarket chain said one of its outlets had been affected.

Ireland’s third-largest supermarket ⁠chain, ⁠SuperValu, said ​refrigeration systems limited ⁠to ​a ‌specific ‌model ‌in 13 of its 223 shops ‌had been affected by ​a cyber-incident, ⁠and that chilled and ​frozen products ​had been removed from ​sale.

Many cyber-attacks involve extortion or are politically motivated and are potentially carried out by state-level actors, said Tom Hegel of the cybersecurity firm SentinelOne. But the supermarket attacks, with no financial demands, point to sabotage, he said.

“Retail is an easy target because retail chains run enormous estates of refrigeration controllers, building management systems, door access panels and point-of-sale gear,” Hegel told Reuters.

Patrick Lamplmair of the cybersecurity firm Tributech said cyber-attackers would keep going “until it stops working” because the method was “cheap and the damage is immediate”. Many refrigeration systems had known and as yet unfixed flaws, he said.

“Thousands of these controllers were still reachable from the internet after the French attack,” he added. “A few commands to a temperature controller can destroy stock overnight and close stores.”

In the French attack, the hackers pirated controllers mostly supplied by the Danish company Danfoss, which said subsequently that it had identified some security flaws last year and had “long recommended” customers install updates.

The hackers remotely overrode the settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets at chains including Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix, pushing them from as low as -27C to well over 50C.

The shops had to discard vast quantities of fresh meat, dairy and frozen products. Individual supermarkets reportedly suffered losses ranging from tens of thousands of euros to more than €130,000 (£109,000).

The Paris prosecutor’s office has opened a formal investigation into the French attack and the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, instructed France’s national cybersecurity agency, Ansii, to investigate.

Gaming_Tech.title: Investors pull billions in funds from Binance after record $6.3bn hack
Gaming_Tech.text:
Investors have pulled $3.6bn (£2.7bn) in funds from the cryptocurrency exchange Binance as it recovers from a record hack in which billions were stolen from customer accounts.

The platform was hit by a $6.3bn theft on Thursday, which has since been described as the biggest heist in history. Experts identified North Korea as the probable culprit.

Binance initially froze withdrawals as it investigated the breach but on Sunday announced it had begun a phased reopening.

By Sunday afternoon, the platform had processed $4.6bn in withdrawals and $1bn in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of about $3.6bn – representing 2.1% of its $171bn in total assets under management.

The numbers were confirmed by the company in its latest proof of reserves snapshot. A full report is expected on Monday.

Binance said: “After an initial spike, withdrawal volumes have declined and are stabilising as expected, while deposit volumes have remained substantial.”

The crypto exchange told its customers that market conditions were stable and that its team was “testing rigorously the remaining networks and assets”.

“We know how important safe and reliable access to your funds is and will share details of the next phase as soon as we can,” it said on X.

In the first phase Binance restored withdrawals for 15 networks and assets, including ethereum, USDT and USDC tokens on the ethereum blockchain, as well as some others held on the BNB Smart Chain blockchain. Later on Sunday, dealing in the Dogecoin and Avalanche currencies resumed on their own platforms.

The platform said it had replenished 90% of the ⁠amount stolen. The remaining 10% of tokens were less liquid, meaning they ⁠may take ​longer to buy, the company said in a post on X on Saturday.

Richard Teng, Binance’s co-chief executive, said separately that the company was “committed to covering the ⁠remaining 10%” and users would not bear the financial impact of the hack.

On Saturday the FBI confirmed earlier suspicions from private investigators and analysts that a North Korea-affiliated group called TraderTraitor was behind the hack.

TraderTraitor is believed to be part of the Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for The Interview, a film that mocked the North Korean leader Kim Jong-un.

“The Federal Bureau of Investigation is releasing information advising the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6bn in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29,” the law enforcement agency said.

The FBI added that it had observed “TraderTraitor actors” converting stolen assets into ethereum, and expected those assets to be laundered further by converting them using decentralised finance and instant swap services.

It said it was urging private sector entities “to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors” were “using to launder these stolen assets”.

Teng said on Friday that the breach was a “complex attack” involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity, making it ‌harder to trace and investigate.

Binance said it had set aside about $6.34bn of company funds to cover the losses. “Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident,” the company said.

The money spent rebuying tokens came from using part of its $1bn secure asset fund for users, a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some ⁠of its futures insurance fund and own corporate treasury, Binance said ​on X.

The hack came as many observers expressed worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.

Bitcoin plunged nearly 5% after the news of the hack, while ethereum dropped nearly 6% and BNB, native to Binance, tumbled nearly 10%.

Gaming_Tech.title: Unions gain access to thousands of Google workers after UK employment rights overhaul
Gaming_Tech.text:
Trade unions are expected to make further inroads into big tech companies in the UK after new rights for unions to access workplaces came into force, with Google UK signing an agreement on Monday.

The Prospect union has reached an agreement with Google to begin organising among about 7,000 workers across its UK operations, including YouTube but excluding DeepMind.

Google DeepMind is expected to strike a separate agreement, with the Communication Workers Union and the Unite union seeking recognition there. The deal follows a similar agreement between Prospect and Meta, which owns Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram and employs about 5,000 people in the UK.

The agreements will allow unions to communicate with non-unionised workers and encourage them to join.

The union, which represents more than 160,000 UK workers across several sectors, will now be able to run sessions inside Google’s workplaces, including the flagship headquarters in King’s Cross, London.

Prospect’s general secretary, Mike Clancy, said: “Prospect has been organising tech workers for many years, and this access agreement is a powerful signal of intent that we can successfully negotiate agreements with even the biggest global tech companies.

“Tech workers deserve a stronger voice at work, whether that is over bread-and-butter trade union issues like pay and flexibility, AI deployment or workplace culture. I am pleased that Google has struck this agreement with us, and hope it sends a clear signal to other tech companies that having a relationship with trade unions is the new normal in the sector.”

He said workers would have a stronger voice as more employees at Google and Meta joined trade unions. “With our track record of delivering wins for members, I am looking forward to seeing what we can achieve together.”

Google said it had signed the access agreement to comply with the new UK workplace legislation, although it maintained that it already had good internal employee relations.

“This step builds on our established work with internal employee representative groups, allowing us to fulfil these new requirements while preserving the respectful, direct dialogue our culture is built on,” a spokesperson said.

Paul Nowak, the TUC general secretary, said last week that he expected a wave of union recognition deals in the private sector over the next year as the “transformative” rules on accessing workplaces came into force.

The Employment Rights Act gives unions the right to enter workplaces to meet workers or communicate with them electronically. From January, employers will be required to inform workers of their right to join a union.

Previously, unions seeking recognition have sometimes had to organise workers from outside their workplaces – as was the case with the GMB’s thwarted effort to gain recognition at Amazon’s warehouse near Coventry two years ago.

Gaming_Tech.title: Palantir AI tech unused or little used by 29 NHS trusts said to be benefiting from it
Gaming_Tech.text:
More than two dozen hospital trusts the NHS claims have benefited from Palantir’s medical data platform are not using all or most of the AI-powered technology, the Guardian can reveal.

The 29 hospital trusts that NHS England publicly lists as “realising benefits” from the controversial £330m federated data platform (FDP) have said the system is not live or they are not using any of its applications. The apparent gap between the NHS claim and the trusts’ understanding was described as “very misleading” by one senior health official.

It comes as the health secretary, Yvette Cooper, faces calls from MPs and campaigners to axe the US tech firm’s contract to deliver the flagship government AI system, which aims to connect scattered medical files, speed up hospital discharges and improve surgery scheduling among other potentially life-saving improvements.

Palantir’s UK and Europe chief executive, Louis Mosley, said ending its contract would be “putting politics above patients” and accused critics of “Palantir Derangement Syndrome”. The company has contracts to supply AI to the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s homeland security crackdown, while its billionaire founder, Peter Thiel, has questioned democracy, said tech companies can “unilaterally change the world” and called technology an “incredible alternative to politics”.

NHS England has previously faced scrutiny over how it has used data to defend the Palantir contract, which began in 2024. It claims 117,539 more operations were carried out by trusts using the FDP in a year, but this summer it conceded it could not prove cause and effect, and the Office for Statistics Regulation (OSR) watchdog ran an investigation. Asked about the claim of NHS Trusts “realising benefits”, the OSR said it will now be “taking this forward under our casework function”.

The contrast between the number of hospitals the NHS claims realise benefits from Palantir’s technology and the statements of the hospitals themselves emerged from more than 100 freedom of information requests. NHS England states on its website that 137 trusts are “live” with the FDP, but of those described as “realising benefits”, 29 responded that they were either not using the system or its apps.

Epsom and St Helier said it was “not using FDP at the moment”, Kent and Medway said the trust “has been focused on other priorities … the FDP is not currently live”, Mersey Care said they had “not yet gone live with the FDP”, Nottingham University Hospitals said “no implementation timeline has been agreed”, and University Hospitals of North Midlands said: “FDP is not live. We do not intend to roll it out in the future.”

Chi Onwurah, chair of the Commons science and technology committee, said: “If many NHS trusts don’t see the value of the FDP, serious questions need to be asked about whether the hype surrounding Palantir’s products matches reality.”

She called on the government to activate the 2027 break clause in Palantir’s contract and launch an open competition for a UK-owned and based supplier to handle patient records. The Commons health select committee is also calling for ministers to pull Palantir’s deal.

The FOIs were obtained by Medact, a medical charity campaigning for Palantir to be ejected from the NHS, and shared with the Guardian. Medact spokesperson Dr Rhiannon Mihranian Osborne said: “Our NHS institutions are meant to work in the interests of public trust and evidence-based healthcare, not use creative accounting to justify a deeply controversial contract. There is no good reason for the government to continue this failing project. We now have to ask, if ministers are using these flawed claims to make their decision, are they being misled?”

Asked to respond, NHS England insisted nearly 140 trusts “have now reported benefits from the wide range of tools available on the platform, helping staff join up and improve care for patients, and work more efficiently.”

It has previously said that its list of hospital trusts reporting benefits includes those using the tools for back office data analysis and submission rather than to support patient care. It is understood trusts that say they do not use the FDP may use a small part of its functionality to help calculate treatment costs. For example, Torbay and South Devon NHS Foundation Trust said it is “not currently operationally using the FDP” but NHS England records it as “live” because infrastructure is in place “to support data submission, rather than active operational use of FDP apps.”

Palantir has been hitting back against criticism of its deal and last month hired Labour’s former deputy leader and member of the House of Lords Tom Watson as a full-time senior lobbyist. Watson this week has been posting videos on X aiming to debunk “myths” about Palantir, including concerns that public services will become “locked in” to its systems. He rebutted criticism from the Green party leader Zack Polanski, who said it was “beyond ridiculous” that Lord Watson was a life peer.

Watson and Mosley have also been writing directly to critical MPs in letters that have counted the times they have spoken out against the company, which one recipient, Labour’s Clive Lewis, described as “very Big Brother”.

Marc Farr, chair of the NHS Chief Data and Analytics Officers Network, said: “I am concerned to hear that there are 29 trusts reported as receiving benefits but when asked are not actually using the tool. It is great that a number of trusts that have adopted the FDP are benefiting from this nationally funded programme, but it is crucial for public support … that benefits are reported accurately, transparently and in a way that can be properly verified.”

A Palantir spokesperson said: “Palantir software is helping to deliver better care, with trusts using it recording 117,000 additional operations, a 14.3% reduction in discharge delays for long stay patients and a 5.6% improvement in the number of people finding out whether or not they have cancer within 28 days.”

Entertainment.title: Channel 4 documentary and journalists 'poisoned the well' against Russell Brand, court hears
Entertainment.text:
Journalists "poisoned the well of justice" by prompting complainants to come forward and make criminal allegations against Russell Brand, jurors have heard.

In his closing speech on Monday, Ian Winter KC, Brand's defence barrister, said a Channel 4 documentary and stories in the Times and Sunday Times that made allegations about Brand in 2023 "caused people who had not previously considered for it to be appropriate to bring criminal allegations against him, to do so, and very many years after."

Brand faces seven counts; three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one allegation of attempted indecent assault.

He denies all the allegations.

On Monday at Southwark Crown Court, Winter told jurors that "living a highly promiscuous life is entirely lawful".

He added: "Can you possibly be sure in this case that out of the many, many women who voluntarily had sex with Mr Brand, that he raped just three of them?"

Winter said it was an "extremely curious feature" of the case that Brand "obviously genuinely believed that they were consenting because that's the only thing that would explain why his behaviour was normal".

He added that there was "no evidence he is some sort of psychopath who rapes people and thinks it's normal".

Referring to one allegation from 1999, Winter said: "You would have to be a psychopath" to be raping someone and "asking if they were enjoying it" at the same time.

"He left her his actual email address. Rapists do not give out their email address," he added.

"Rapists do not leave their photographs. Rapists do not kiss their victims goodbye."

Referring to the Channel 4 Dispatches documentary, which made allegations about Brand in 2023, Winter reminded jurors that the judge in the trial had directed them that the programme was "very one-sided" and "produced in a dramatic manner".

The barrister said it was "published without a single journalist ever speaking to Mr Brand about it other than to protect their defamation risk... protect their right to reply after the programme had been made".

He later said: "Most importantly, that programme and those allegations in it - Mr Brand is innocent of them.

"So, they poisoned the well in respect of things of which Mr Brand is innocent."

He added that the six complainants in the case were "not random", adding they were "thoroughly contaminated by the programme".

Jurors were reminded about what Brand had said in his evidence about the impact the programme had on him.

Winter said one "graphic" example of the "truly devastating effect" on Brand was when a hospital "would not permit him to visit the bedside of his baby son after life-saving open heart surgery".

Winter said: "That tells you the extent to which public opinion has... corrupted."

Brand previously told jurors that Great Ormond Street Hospital didn't let him stay with his son due to "material that had been published in the public eye".

Brand's lawyer also told jurors that Brand "had an immense amount of sex", but that "none of it was unlawful".

"Disgusting, distasteful, immoral, who cares?" he added.

"It's irrelevant to your consideration."

Winter said he was "sorry to have to say it's not criminal to treat women unkindly before, during or after sex," nor is it "criminal to be disrespectful, or be rude, or to behave like a crazy idiot."

He also questioned how none of the women came forward during the MeToo movement.

"Many women were questioning whether they had a bad experience sexually at the hands of a famous person. It could not have been more publicised," he said.

"How is it that not one of them thought what happened to them involved a crime during the MeToo movement?"

Speaking about Brand's comedy, Winter described it as "radical and different" as Brand was "telling the truth about what was going on consensually between adults".

The barrister said: "You may think that while his comedy was certainly not to all tastes and very much the product of the time, he was honest then about it, he was honest then about what sort of sex he was engaged in."

He said Brand's stand-up comedy was focused on him "telling the truth", adding: "When you put yourself back to the time, it was radical and different because someone was telling the truth about what's going on consensually between adults."

Winter also referred to evidence given by Brand's wife Laura, saying: "She fell in love with that man in full knowledge of what he was doing.

"She married him, she bore him three children."

He went on to say that she would not have done so if Brand was "guilty as charged".

Brand arrived at court today accompanied by his wife Laura and her father Bernard Gallacher, the former professional golfer.

The trial continues.

Entertainment.title: Martha Stewart says she 'really screwed up' with Halloween homeless costume
Entertainment.text:
Veteran lifestyle guru Martha Stewart has admitted she "really screwed up" by dressing as a homeless person for Halloween.

The 85-year-old US entrepreneur and personality has deleted a photo of herself wearing torn clothes and dirt on her face, holding a sign saying: "I am hungry help me!!"

She posted a statement on Sunday saying she was "distressed that my Halloween costume yesterday, which was intended to bring more awareness to the very serious subject of homelessness, has offended people, which was never my intention".

That was followed by a fuller apology. "It's hard to admit when you've really screwed up. My earlier statement didn't go far enough. I know many people are suffering economically. Wearing a costume like I did was insensitive and not funny. I am very sorry."

Stewart had captioned her original Instagram photo: "My QVC candles are perfect for Halloween!!!"

The post received a swift and sharp backlash.

"This sartorial take on a homeless person is a lot. Insulting? Demeaning? Confusing? All of the above," PR expert Molly McPherson wrote, external.

One person wrote on social media: "Why in the hell would you even think about wearing that as a costume?"

Another said: "Why would she do that? Who did she think would find that funny? Billionaires?"

Arguably the original lifestyle influencer, Stewart started a catering business in the 1970s and rose to fame in the 1990s when she started her own magazine, Martha Stewart Living.

She later became a billionaire, albeit briefly, when her media empire Martha Stewart Living Omnimedia was floated on the stock market in 1999.

But in 2004 she was sentenced to five months in prison after she was found guilty on a number of charges related to an insider trading scandal.

She has since attempted to rebuild her brand, starring in her own reality television show, expanding her food products and teaming up with rapper and friend Snoop Dogg for a television series.

In 2015, she sold Martha Stewart Living Omnimedia for more than $350m (£220m).

Entertainment.title: Celebrity Traitors: Why the real winners are Maya Jama, King Kenny and Miranda Hart
Entertainment.text:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from The Celebrity Traitors final

In some ways, all the players on The Celebrity Traitors can be seen as winners.

They all got to appear on a hugely popular TV show, rubbing shoulders with other stars and gaining new fans along the way.

But there are certain celebrities, such as Miranda Hart, King Kenny, Maya Jama and Joanne McNally, who have been tipped by industry experts as getting the biggest career boost after the show.

Sebastian "Bash" Croft - who won the game, alongside Romesh Ranganathan - could also now be in line for greater roles.

We've taken a look at the breakout stars of the series and what might lie ahead for them.

After a spell of ill-health, the show has done wonders for bringing Miranda Hart back into the public eye.

There was that incredible “Little Mix Big Mix” viral dance moment, but Hart also displayed a level of vulnerability which stood out in a show where the stars don't really talk about their personal lives.

When her friend Joe Lycett was banished, her tearful reaction to his exit provided a rare poignant moment.

"Connection and laughter and joy are bigger than this game - and to meet someone and just play and laugh, it's all us humans need, you know?" she said.

When she was murdered, she also demonstrated genuine emotion in her response. "Ultimately, in my little personal story, this has been quite extraordinary," she said.

For culture journalist Natalie Jamieson, Hart's openness and relatability made her the "standout" star from this year's series.

And it could also lead to us seeing more of Hart on the small screen. According to The Sun, external, the BBC is looking to bring back her self-titled sitcom after her stint on Celebrity Traitors led to fresh interest in the show.

The BBC declined to comment on the possible return of Hart’s show.

But she’s not the only one who won hearts by showing real warmth.

The same could be said for Romesh Ranganathan - who, in a departure from his usual cynical, deadpan stand-up persona, seemed really to care about his fellow cast members. Jerry Hall also won viewers over with her charming eccentricity.

And then there’s James Acaster, who showed genuine vulnerability as he struggled to come to terms with being a traitor.

Social media users seemed split after his bombshell confession to being a traitor, with some totally exasperated and others saying they respected him for going out on his own terms.

Either way, he's definitely got the nation talking.

When it comes to celebrities who are most likely to see the biggest career boost, most experts say Kenny is King.

Going into the castle, the 29-year-old was best known to younger fans as a member of the popular British YouTube collective Beta Squad.

But Kenny will have been "the least familiar name to a mainstream audience," says showbiz journalist Nikki Onafuye.

That all changed as he was recruited as a traitor, bringing much-needed energy to the turret - and he made it all the way through to Friday night’s tense final.

Having shown he can hold his own alongside established broadcasters, actors and comedians, big things could now be in store for Kenny.

"He 100% has just been minted as a mainstream star now," said Marina Hyde, on The Rest is Entertainment podcast.

“The next steps could be panel shows, presenting roles, reality competitions or entertainment formats,” adds TV reporter Siobhan Synnot.

Fellow traitor Maya Jama also sailed all the way to the final with her cool-as-a-cucumber persona making her a traitor to be reckoned with.

Despite being banished in dramatic fashion, she could now be in line to receive £1m per deal, according to a report in The Times earlier this week, external.

What Celebrity Traitors has done for Jama is allow her to reveal more of her personality than on Love Island, says Onafuye.

But TV reporter Synnot thinks between the two, Kenny has more to gain because he has introduced himself to millions of new viewers - whereas Jama was already one of Britain's best-known TV presenters before Celebrity Traitors.

"Maya's gain is subtler: she can emerge looking less like the presenter of Love Island and more like a genuinely versatile television star," she says.

Of all the comedians in the castle, Joanne McNally was initially the least well known, says Caroline Frost, TV editor at Radio Times.

But she flourished on the show, lasting right up to Thursday's semi-final.

"And she's taken her own path, ignoring the herd and making her own voting decisions, sometimes chaotically, but always with charm, wit and good humour,” says Frost.

The Irish comedian's podcast was already popular before the show.

But after her stint as the joker of the pack, bigger things could now lie in store for her.

Just a few days ago, it was announced, external that her stand-up tour has been extended into 2027, "due to phenomenal demand".

And her agents will be "fielding calls" for her to bring her star power to other shows, adds Frost.

Culture journalist Jamieson says some of the other female contestants - such as Sharon Rooney, Leigh-Anne Pinnock and Myha'la - also stood out for showing their wit and wisdom, which could serve them well in the outside world.

Things got a bit awkward in one of the episodes, when Sharon disagreed with some of the cast on a challenge, with some social media users saying she was acting in a "childish" way.

But others argued it was a classic case of women being drowned out by men.

"There's been a subtlety in the smartness of women on display here, alongside the frustration of not always being listened to in the game," says Jamieson.

In the end, it was faithful duo Romesh Ranganathan and Sebastian ‘Bash’ Croft who emerged victorious.

Comedian Ranganathan was already a huge star, but the show has introduced Croft, 24, to a much wider audience.

He’s had previous acting roles in Game of Thrones and Heartstopper, but Traitors allowed him to show his own personality, "which as we've seen has endeared him both to other players and the huge watching audience", says Frost.

He is also building his career as a pop star, and he's had a strong presence on social media during the series, posting videos of his tracks.

His debut EP comes out later in November, perfect timing to capitalise on his Traitors win.

What's clear is that the true victors aren't necessarily the ones who get their hands on the prize pot.

Arguably, what matters most is the amount of screen time you get - and what you do with it.

On that note, spare a thought for those who left the show early, such as Amol Rajan, Julie Hesmondhalgh and Hannah Fry.

But all made an impact in their own way and, as Synnot points out, they get "a nice anecdote" for future interviews.

And what of James Blunt, who stole hearts with his military approach to the challenges and eccentric Top Gun-style outfits - and who came so close to winning the whole show?

Maybe he's the mystery man in contention for the new James B(ond) - although his hapless theories could mean he'll be in line to be the new Johnny English instead.

Entertainment.title: Jack Lowden says James Bond speculation is 'flattering'
Entertainment.text:
Slow Horses star Jack Lowden has described the speculation he could be the next James Bond as "flattering".

The 36-year-old - who grew up in Oxton in the Scottish Borders - has been reported to be in the running for the role alongside Callum Turner and Josh O'Connor.

The actor chosen will replace Daniel Craig, who took over the role of Bond with Casino Royale in 2006 and bowed out after his fifth film, No Time To Die, in 2021.

Speaking to GQ Hype, external, Lowden responded to the rumours - but did not confirm or deny whether he was part of the auditioning process.

"On this… it's all very flattering," he said.

"It's nice to be mentioned – for any role – and I'm just not really going to add to the noise," he said.

Last month, his Slow Horses co-star Gary Oldman claimed the new Bond had been chosen, adding that he had his "fingers crossed" for Lowden.

Speaking to Canada's Global, Oldman said: "It's been rumoured that he's on the shortlist.

"We're going to find out pretty soon, aren't we? Because they have picked him.

"They have made their choice, but they have not announced it yet. So my fingers are crossed for Jack."

When asked about Oldman's comments, Lowden said: "It's very nice, and Gary's a sweetheart – it's particularly lovely, coming from someone like him.

"But I don't really listen to it."

He added: "As a young male actor, generally, the minute you're not playing a zany artist type, the minute you're in a suit, people fling it at you."

During an appearance at the Toronto International Film Festival, Oldman clarified his remarks and said he had only heard a rumour that producers had selected an actor from a shortlist, not that Lowden had been cast.

He said he did not know who had got the part but he was hoping it was his co-star.

Lowden is best known for his roles in films including Dunkirk and Mary Queen Of Scots, as well as TV roles in Slow Horses and War and Peace.

The actor has also been awarded two Baftas and a Laurence Olivier Award as well as nominations for two Primetime Emmy Awards and a Golden Globe Award.

He is next starring alongside Emma Corrin in Dolly Alderton's adaptation of Pride And Prejudice.

The next Bond film is in development after it was announced last year that Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight would write the script.

Amy Pascal and David Heyman will produce the upcoming project, which is currently untitled, while Dune's Denis Villeneuve will direct.

Pascal told Deadline earlier this year that a casting announcement by the end of the year was a "good bet" but that Craig was a "hard act to follow".

Entertainment.title: Jamal Edwards' sister on the 20-year legacy of SBTV
Entertainment.text:
Launched in the early days of YouTube with homemade videos featuring emerging artists, online music channel SBTV went on to shake up the music industry.

Pioneering DJ and entrepreneur Jamal Edwards founded the grime and rap music platform back in 2006 after he got a camcorder for Christmas and started filming his friends on the council estate where he grew up in west London.

It helped launch the careers of many acts including Dave, Ed Sheeran, Jessie J and Skepta.

By the age of 23, Jamal was a multimillionaire and channelling his success into helping others. He was awarded an MBE for his services to music in 2014.

He died aged 31 in 2022 of cardiac arrhythmia following drug use, prompting a flood of tributes from those who he helped support.

As the channel marks its 20th anniversary, it is set to bring back some of its freestyle formats in the hope of discovering a new generation of rappers.

His sister has been keeping his legacy going by taking over as CEO of SBTV.

Tanisha, who is also a singer-songwriter and producer, feels in a world where algorithms influence what we listen to, it's important to still have platforms curated by music lovers.

"I know how it feels as an artist and trying to put yourself out there and break through those doors," she says.

"So I think it's very key to still have a platform that does want to help up-and-coming talent, that does want to go to places on the map that you wouldn't mainly really go to."

A host of the artists who were platformed on the channel, including Tinie Tempah, Lady Leshurr and Tinchy Stryder, are also set to perform at a one-off show held in London's O2 arena next week to mark the 20-year milestone.

The event, which will also see artists like Dappy, Headie One and Ms Banks take to the stage, will raise money for the Jamal Edwards Self Belief Trust.

Tanisha says being able to honour her brother's legacy "means everything".

"Obviously he's not physically here with us," she says.

"But to be able to carry on his name and carry on the work he did and be able to push his message of self-belief.

"And finding the next generation of talent, working with all these artists that he's previously worked with... I just feel really grateful, honoured and blessed that we're able to continue his name and legacy in such a way."

Rappers Nolay and Griminal are among those who see Jamal as a "catalyst" for their careers and say they're excited to celebrate his impact at the upcoming show.

Griminal recalls how the DJ had a "positive energy and spirit" and an eye for spotting "raw talent".

Nolay tells Newsbeat Jamal not only championed her work, but opened her eyes to the power of promoting your music online and creating a brand for yourself.

Boosting yourself on social media to break into the music industry has become a given in 2026 - something Nolay says has made things feel less "real".

"We're in a day and time where the connection's kind of being lost because of evolution and technology," Nolay says.

"But what happens is authenticity becomes lost along the way by doing that.

"And to have something like SBTV there and revert back to what Jamal was doing in the first place, it's gonna [be] such a large platform for artists that feel disheartened."

You can hear more about SBTV's legacy from the team's takeover on DJ Target's show on BBC Sounds.

Entertainment.title: The Voice UK winner Cate McHugh says she wanted to be Taylor Swift growing up
Entertainment.text:
The winner of the Voice UK says she decided "I was going to be Taylor Swift" as a teenager after being given a guitar, before busking on the streets of Cardiff.

Welsh singer Cate McHugh was crowned the winner of the show on Saturday, after being mentored by "the legend that is Sir Tom Jones".

McHugh, from Llantwit Major, in the Vale of Glamorgan, said Sir Tom was so warm and supportive that it felt "as if you've known him for years".

One of the standout pieces of advice he gave to her early on was to focus on the story being told in the song, she explained.

McHugh said that when she found herself getting "a little bit flappy and excited" while rehearsing Sir Tom would say "nope, what's the story?", and urged her to focus on that and "stay true".

The 32-year-old, who began her career as a teenager busking under the watchful eye of her parents, said she and Sir Tom had "really lovely interactions and a lovely comfortable connection" and that it was "just an honour to be in his presence".

The final was a poignant moment for Sir Tom as it was his last appearance on the show, having been a coach on and off since it began in 2012.

He made headlines in September after revealing that ITV had "made the decision" to "fire" him from the show's coaching panel.

McHugh said that in the moments before she was announced as the winner, she felt "super peaceful because I was so happy with where I'd come" in the show.

The singer, who has a six-year-old daughter and a 16-year-old stepson, said she felt confetti on her shoulder and "opened my eyes and thought 'oh my God, they said my name'."

She said she wanted to thank her family, including her husband Nathan, for surrounding her with "all of that love" and support throughout the show and during the final.

Recalling her early days of performing, McHugh said "I was the kid who was always singing and my parents decided very early on that if they didn't put me in singing lessons this was going to get really annoying really quickly".

She was gifted an acoustic guitar for her birthday around the time Taylor Swift released her album Fearless, and "decided that I was going to be Taylor Swift, I was going to learn the entire album from start to finish".

Aged 15, she told her parents she wanted to busk in Cardiff and "they did everything they could to fulfil that happening in the safest way which did mean, apparently, my father was lingering around on Queen Street, just keeping an eye on me".

Busking and taking requests from passers-by helped her to gain confidence and she has "paid my dues since then", including singing on cruise ships, McHugh said.

McHugh said that navigating losing her sight aged 22 due to degenerative macular condition Stargardt disease, external had made her more determined to succeed.

She said music had "always been an outlet, emotionally, as so many musicians will say, but for me, when I'm on a stage singing and the lights are down on the audience, it's the one place that I don't think about my sight loss".

McHugh said that "as long as I know the words and I'm not trying to read them off an iPad then I'm absolutely there in that moment".

She described her sight loss as "just a small part of me, it's not who I am".

McHugh added that while many people with differences and disabilities sometimes felt they had to make themselves smaller "so that you don't become a nuisance to people", she chose "to find a way to take up space and be bigger and that's where music took me".

She is now working on her first original song in a studio which should be released "relatively soon, hopefully, fingers crossed".

Footage shared by McHugh on social media after her win showed her laughing and smiling with family and friends screaming in delight as they celebrated her victory at a watch party in Cardiff.

She has won a £50,000 cash prize and a recording contract, with her first ever single, a cover of The Beatles classic Blackbird, now released.

Entertainment.title: Outlander impact celebrated with special Bafta Scotland award
Entertainment.text:
The team behind the historic-fantasy TV series Outlander are to be honoured by Bafta Scotland for their contributions to the industry.

Sam Heughan, who played Jacobite soldier Jamie Fraser, is one of four members of the show's production team who will get the Outstanding Contribution to Television award at a ceremony later this month.

Outlander ended in the summer after a 12-year run spanning eight seasons.

The awards body said Outlander has had an "undeniable" impact on Scotland's screen industry while also providing opportunities for local talent.

Throughout the show's run, more than 170 trainee roles were created through an initiative led by the production team.

Scotland's tourist agency has also heralded the impact of the "Outlander effect" for boosting the country's image on the world stage, with thousands of visitors now saying they have come to Scotland to see the landscapes seen in TV and film productions.

Alongside Heughan and his co-star Catriona Balfe, who played his time-travelling love interest, two other executive producers will be given the special Bafta award.

Ronald D. Moore will receive it for his role in adapting the story from Diana Gabaldon's original novels into the TV format.

He said: "It has been a tremendous pleasure to work with our Scottish crew, to utilise the Scottish locations and to learn more about Scottish culture and history.

"It's been a huge joy for all of us on the production."

American showrunner Matthew B. Roberts added: "When we first landed in Scotland, we were outsiders – Sassenachs – strangers in a strange land telling a very Scottish story.

"What we found was a country that opened its doors and a crew that opened their hearts.

"They welcomed us, guided us when we needed it, and made us feel like we belonged.

"Thirteen years on and I don't feel like a visitor when I step off the plane; I feel like I'm home."

Entertainment.title: Celebrity Traitors comes to a climax in nail-biting final
Entertainment.text:
Spoiler warning: This story reveals details of The Celebrity Traitors final

We've had four weeks of suspense, suspicion and very suspect tactics, as some of Britain's biggest stars engaged in a battle of wits to win the most popular show on TV.

The second series of BBC One's The Celebrity Traitors reached its climax on Friday, with the 21 original contestants having been reduced to seven before the final.

They were then whittled down to two winners - with the faithful duo of comedian Romesh Ranganathan and Heartstopper actor Sebastian "Bash" Croft emerging victorious.

The players successfully banished the remaining traitors - Love Island host Maya Jama and YouTuber King Kenny - in dramatic fashion, and the winning pair shared the £83,000 prize for their charities.

The finale drew an average audience of 11.2 million live viewers, and that number will rise when catch-up is included. Other recent episodes have been watched by more than 15 million, including catch-up.

Kenny reached the final stage, the endgame, after turning on his fellow traitor Maya at the last round table.

Kenny, Romesh and Bash were joined by singer James Blunt in the climax of the endgame, where the remaining contestants gather around a fire pit to decide whether they think there are any traitors left.

When James and Kenny were tied in a vote for who was a traitor, Bash persuaded Romesh to banish Kenny instead of James - thereby securing victory for team faithful.

"Absolutely devastated. Almost scraped it," Kenny seethed. "I was so close, I smelled the victory."

However, he can take consolation from the fact his performance on the show has established him as a mainstream star.

In a further twist, James chose another round of voting and was subsequently evicted himself, leaving Romesh and Bash as the last men standing.

"This might actually be the best day of my life," said 24-year-old Bash through tears of joy.

He, too, can expect a major career boost.

Romesh reflected: "I just really hope my mum's proud. And also my youngest son Charlie, who wanted me to come on the show - dad won. Please show me some respect."

The pair will split their winnings between two refugee charities, the Refugee Council and Choose Love.

Earlier, actor Michael Sheen was murdered in the first action of Friday's episode. "I am incredibly disappointed," he said. "Gutted that I got so close to the end. It's been absolutely unforgettable."

When it came to the endgame, Little Mix singer Leigh-Anne Pinnock was swiftly banished after Kenny voted to remove her.

"I was thinking me and him had a mutual understanding, and now I feel so stupid," she raged.

"But I'm walking away feeling super proud and like I've really accomplished something here."

Meanwhile, James B was left rueing one final mistake in a long but valiant catalogue of misjudgements throughout the series.

The singer, who looked aghast when he was attacked by Romesh during the endgame, was then the only one to choose to banish again when it came to the final three.

James was unaware that Romesh and Bash had both chosen to end the game - meaning he too could have been a winner if he had done the same - but became the victim of his own choice to banish.

"I've loved trying to work it out, I've loved getting it wrong so often, I've loved the tiny moments when I've got it right," he said wistfully. "I've loved the game."

There have been reports, external that filming of the scene was paused and he was checked by welfare staff after he became anxious.

Asked about the reports, a BBC spokesperson said on Friday that the safety and welfare of those taking part was the "highest priority", and "players are closely monitored and supported throughout by production which includes a dedicated and experienced welfare team".

Speculation about the round table being heavily edited was fuelled when eagle-eyed viewers noticed, external a shot of Romesh reacting in shock - apparently to James A's initial confession - which in fact seemed to have come from a later moment, after Romesh had voted for James by writing his name on the blackboard.

In the episode, the sequence where the celebrities all voted for James in light of his admission was shown as a relatively quick and straightforward process, raising a question about what prompted Romesh's shocked look.

Acaster did not take part in Friday's edition of spin-off show Uncloaked, which reunited some of the celebrity contestants following the final.

The comedian's bombshell the previous night did provide the programme with a twist to spark it to life after what some viewers saw as a mid-series lull.

On Thursday, the Hollywood Reporter noted, external that the show had achieved record-breaking ratings - before asking: "Why, then, has much of the consensus on social media been that it's all felt a bit dull?"

Some noted a shortage of true back-stabbing, double-crossing and explosive rows - the things, in other words, that viewers love the most - while the celebrities were more chummy and savvy than previous groups of castle dwellers.

And while there was no shortage of big characters, this season lacked an equivalent to Alan Carr, the hugely popular and apparently hapless comedian who lied and murdered his way to an unlikely victory as a traitor last year.

The drama ramped up in the final, though, and Friday's episode is likely to have been the most watched TV programme of the year.

Entertainment.title: 'Respected and beloved': Tributes pour in for Sir Patrick Stewart
Entertainment.text:
Sir Ian McKellen has led tributes to Sir Patrick Stewart following his death at the age of 86, calling him "the most respected and beloved actor of his generation".

Tributes to the renowned British actor have poured in since his death at his Los Angeles home after "a brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy Body Dementia was announced on Thursday.

"He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and, in my case, love," Sir Ian, Sir Patrick's X-Men co-star, said.

Famous for his role as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek, Sir Patrick was a versatile actor who won multiple awards, balancing Hollywood roles and a career in classical theatre.

William Shatner, who also helmed the USS Enterprise in Star Trek, said Sir Patrick brought "intelligence, grace and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did".

"Captain Picard stood for the best of us and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work," Shatner added.

Stewart depicted Picard in more than 170 episodes of the hit sci-fi TV series between 1987 and 1994, as well as in four feature films. He returned to the role for Star Trek: Picard in 2020.

Dame Judi Dench said she was "shocked" and "very sad" to hear of Sir Patrick's death, adding: "He's never been one of those actors who never felt like it that night, he was always very, very committed... He'll be much missed and he was much admired."

George Takei, who played Hikaru Sulu in Star Trek, said the actor "inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity".

Sir Patrick would later be celebrated for his portrayal of Professor Charles Xavier - most commonly known as Professor X - in the X-Men film franchise.

Hugh Jackman, who starred alongside him in the franchise, called him a "tremendous friend and man", saying: "We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today."

Sir Ian, a longtime friend of his X-Men co-star, who officiated his wedding in 2013, said Sir Patrick was "defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire".

"You could hear it in his accented voice and in the stern honesty with which he told you what he thought and felt. Yorkshiremen have no truck with half-truths or avoidance of big issues."

Sir Ian recalled first meeting Sir Patrick as young actors in the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC) and how he had expressed caution over him taking on the Star Trek role.

"He took the risk and thank goodness for us all that he did," said Sir Ian, who appeared with Sir Patrick in a 2009 theatre production of Waiting for Godot.

He added that while the US had become Sir Patrick's "adopted home", he "never forsook his origins" growing up in Yorkshire, and said "the proudest achievement of the most respected and beloved actor of his generation on either side of the Atlantic, was his appointment as chancellor of Huddersfield University".

Sir Ian noted that Sir Patrick's final film appearance will be as Professor X in the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday film. Marvel Studios described him as "a singular talent, a generous collaborator and a true gentleman".

The Academy dubbed his voice "unmistakable", adding: "Whether commanding the bridge of the Enterprise or guiding a generation of young mutants, Sir Patrick Stewart brought a tenderness to his characters that made us feel we knew them."

Sir Patrick died on Wednesday "in the loving care of his wife", a statement from his family said. "We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace," it added.

The veteran actor is survived by his wife, Sunny Ozell, as well as by his two adult children from his first marriage, Daniel and Sophie Stewart.

Born in the town of Mirfield in 1940, Sir Patrick's love of drama began at school where he was introduced to Shakespeare and his first public performance was in a local church production of Cinderella.

He threw himself enthusiastically into the flourishing local theatre. "I used to recite Shakespeare from memory," he said. "I just learned all these big speeches."

When Sir Patrick was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010, he said he owed "literally everything" to his former English teacher who first encouraged him to perform.

His first foray into professional acting was when he joined the RSC in 1966, going on to play King John, Oberon in A Midsummer Night's Dream and Henry IV.

The RSC described him as a "colossus of both stage and screen", remembering him as "one of the finest classical Shakespearean actors of his generation" whose contribution to the company was "beyond measure".

Dame Harriet Walter, who first met Sir Patrick in his theatre days more than 40 years ago, said his passing was like a "huge giant tree has fallen in the forest".

"He had fire in his eyes and you were absolutely in the room with him," the Succession actress told BBC Newsnight. "I've never heard a bad word against him. And I think the world's going to be very poor without him."

Theatres in London's West End will dim their lights for two minutes on 3 November in his honour.

Hannah Essex, co-chief of the Society of London Theatre and UK Theatre, called him "one of the greatest stage actors this country has ever seen".

As well as having roles in films such as Safe House, Robin Hood: Men in Tights and the original Dune, Sir Patrick continued to appear on TV throughout his career, making guest appearances on Frasier, Futurama and the Simpsons.

US actor and animator Seth MacFarlane, who grew up as a fan of Sir Patrick, said he was "gifted the privilege of becoming a colleague and friend" as they worked together on Family Guy, American Dad! and Ted.

MacFarlane described him as a "rare actor who could take any bit of dialogue and elevate it, making a good writer sound great and a great writer sound masterful".

Comedian Ricky Gervais, whose BBC programme Extras Sir Patrick guest starred in, described him as a "legend".

Sharing a video of the pair giggling in a set of bloopers for the series, Gervais said: "I still can't believe he agreed to do this scene. And he didn't even mind when I ruined every take."

Sir Patrick was a lifelong supporter of English Football League club Huddersfield Town, which called him a "titan of his craft".

"Fiercely proud of his Yorkshire roots, Sir Patrick was a Terrier in every sense, and we're proud to have counted him as one of our own," the club added.

Alzheimer's is the most common type of dementia, while Lewy Body Dementia is another common form caused by abnormal protein deposits, which cause a loss of cognitive function.

The Alzheimer's Society CEO Michelle Dyson said Sir Patrick was an "extraordinarily talented and much-loved actor, admired by millions around the world", adding: "His death is a heartbreaking reminder of the devastating impact dementia has on people and families across the globe."

The actor became a campaigner on domestic violence in later life, including becoming an ambassador for domestic abuse charity Refuge in 2007, after witnessing his mother suffer violence at the hands of his father.

Hetti Barkworth-Nanton, Refuge's board chair, said it had been a privilege to "watch his endless devotion" to the cause, adding that he "broke down barriers and taboos on the subject".

Andy Burnham considered Sir Patrick to be "one of the very best" who "never forgot his working-class Yorkshire roots".

"He brought joy to millions," the prime minister's spokesman said on his behalf. "He always stood up for what he believed in, including through his campaigning to help those affected by domestic violence.

Entertainment.title: Party Rock Anthem singer Lauren Bennett struggled with mental health, inquest finds
Entertainment.text:
A British singer who was a member of the girl group G.R.L took her own life, an inquest has found.

Lauren Bennett, 36, who also featured on LMFAO's 2011 hit Party Rock Anthem, was found dead in Kent on 29 May.

In a statement read out by an assistant coroner on Friday, her husband Kenny Wormald said she had been struggling with severe mental health issues before her death.

The court heard she told him she was going out for a walk on the morning of her death while he remained in bed half asleep.

When she did not return for a few hours and did not answer calls or texts from him and multiple other family members, Wormald and her father went looking for her.

He went to a rural location using Find My iPhone for Bennett's device where he found her body.

The professional dancer said the pair talked about everything and there was no indication she was going to end her life.

Her father, Richard Bennett, said his daughter had lived an "amazing life" in a statement read out by assistant coroner Jyoti Gill.

He said she signed a record deal at just 17 and moved to the US on her own.

Pages of farewell notes were later found at her home, Kent and Medway Coroners' Court heard.

Bennett had previously been diagnosed with Fragile X syndrome, a genetic disorder that can cause anxiety, mood instability and depression, it was also told.

In the January before her death, the musician did not sleep for a number of days and was admitted to hospital under a mental health section.

She had experienced "substantial psychological suffering" since this point, Gill noted.

Entertainment.title: Tomb Raider’s creators on how the game changed their lives: ‘Skint staff were suddenly pulling up in sports cars’
Entertainment.text:
Paul Douglas, lead programmer and co-creator

I joined Core Design in the summer of 1994 and met Toby Gard, who showed me his concept sketches for Tomb Raider. He’d already come up with the title and drawn a mock-up box cover with a woman holding two pistols.

I was working on a golf game called The Scottish Open when Toby persuaded me that we should pitch his idea to Jeremy Heath-Smith, Core’s co-founder, who gave us the go-ahead to make a prototype. If I had stuck to the golf game, I would have had a much easier life.

We had a couple of brainstorming sessions, and settled on the game’s four main pillars: platforming, puzzles, combat and story. Combat was always the weakest element but we didn’t have time to improve it. We also came up with the plot and level themes, and whittled a long list of interesting archaeological locations, including Petra and Angkor Wat, down to four: Peru, Greece, Egypt and Atlantis.

Lara was originally Latina and her appearance was more realistic, almost androgynous. We felt that more stylised movement would play better, so her physique changed to reflect that. She became a British mercenary and then, thanks to scriptwriter Vicky Arnold, an aristocrat who tracks down historical artefacts just for fun.

Toby and I came up with the movement metrics by measuring out a hopscotch grid in the car park. Lara was three paces tall and each block in the game’s environment was four paces. All of the gameplay systems grew from those measurements and constraints.

It was brutal getting it delivered on time. I took just three days of holiday in two years. Toby and I were in the office until 2 or 3am every day, including weekends, for the best part of a year. Toby made himself sick with the stress.

We were on the cusp of 3D games going mainstream and the action-adventure focus made us somewhat unique. Then the marketability of Lara thrust Tomb Raider into the stratosphere. The game’s publisher, Eidos Interactive, took the character and ran with it. I like to think the quality of the game spoke for itself, regardless of the way Lara was sexualised.

We never imagined Tomb Raider would blow up in the way it did. It was the right time, right place, and it was different from the competition. We showed that ideas that go against conventional wisdom – a female character will never sell! – can uncover new territory and find success. It was gratifying and humbling to see our hard work rewarded by so many people playing the game. We managed to bottle lightning, although I’m still carrying the scars of its creation.

Heather Stevens, level designer

We developed most of Tomb Raider in a big Victorian building on Ashbourne Road in Derby. We sat there sweating our guts out in the summer and freezing cold in the winter. I was the only female developer, but that didn’t faze me. I felt respected and was almost seen as a sister by some – the team was like a family. It was a defining time in my life.

Toby was lovely. Very eccentric and a bit of a genius. He’d put together a demo that was like a simple top-down version of Prince of Persia, with an Indiana Jones-like character jumping and tumbling from platforms. Although management thought no one would want to play a female character, they went with it. There’s a certain empathy you get from playing Lara. It’s probably the number of times she dies and that awful scream. She was taciturn and mysterious: a loner who played her own game and didn’t answer to anybody. Women hadn’t really been portrayed like that before.

Giving Lara pistols enabled us to show off her acrobatic movement. She was mostly pursued by animals rather than people. Hearing a bat, or the growl of a bear, was much scarier than a gunshot. You felt at the mercy of the wild. And we pushed the 3D environment to its limits. We only had so much memory and processor speed, but we were clever with it, giving players the sense that they were in this vast, cavernous space that was actually lots of rooms bolted together.

Before designing a level, we always had a team meeting where we’d come up with a rough schematic. We all enjoyed history. We chucked in whatever myths and legends we thought would be fun and interesting. Our imaginations ran wild – to the point where we threw a T rex into Peru!

Eidos saw the potential of Lara, rather than the game, so they focused on her. That was the right thing to do, but I think it went a bit too far with what she was wearing or the poses she was put in for some marketing campaigns. They showed a lack of imagination by oversexualising her.

I knew we’d made a great game, but it didn’t really sink in until I saw the sales figures. It was life-changing for all of us. People who were skint before were suddenly pulling up in sports cars. I was able to buy a house from the royalties.

Lara is right up there with iconic characters such as Mario and Sonic the Hedgehog. Feeling as if you’ve left a mark, and connected with millions of people through something you’ve created, is amazing.

Entertainment.title: Beaches, Beatles and a broken marriage: how Wilhelmina Barns-Graham became a radical art icon
Entertainment.text:
At the centre of Tate St Ives’ newly opened retrospective of the British modernist Wilhelmina Barns-Graham, her monumental altar-piece Glacier (Blue Cave) pulls viewers into its frozen tendons of turquoise and white. Its mouth is agape and the blue slit of its eye casts downwards to the rest of its body. The glacier feels human: a vivisection of rock, ice and snow that brings to mind the fragmented facial features of Picasso’s Weeping Woman.

Standing in front of this glassy colossus, the exhibition’s curator, Katy Norris, talks about these “mangled” and “twisted” forms – so alive on the canvas. “Barns-Graham was so distinct in her approach,” Norris says. “There are always questions of: what am I seeing? What is in front of me really? And how does that relate to what I feel inside?”

Glacier (Blue Cave) was painted not far from this gallery space in 1950 – only 10 years after the Scottish-born painter moved 500 miles south to the tiny fishing town of St Ives – but it goes some way to showing just how radical she was over the course of her eight-decade career. From her early 20s, Barns-Graham’s quest for connection saw the self-described “lone wolf” become a key player in the St Ives school which congregated in and around the Cornish harbour during the second world war. She continued to experiment relentlessly with colour, geometry, kineticism and repetition until her death in 2004, aged 91.

Anne Barlow, director of Tate St Ives, points out this major retrospective – the first to span Barns-Graham’s full career – is a “long-overdue celebration” of an expressive master. The art historian Virginia Button wrote that “Barns-Graham clearly felt that as a woman she had been unfairly sidelined from the history of St Ives” with its focus on Ben Nicholson, Peter Lanyon and Patrick Heron. She had a brief period of fame in the 1950s, but it waned in the 1960s as her landscape modernist work became increasingly “hard-edged” (as Rob Airey, director of the Wilhelmina Barns-Graham Trust, puts it) and more daring; less commercial and harder to categorise.

With her “blue eyes that flashed like knives” (so her husband, the writer David Lewis, remarked) and her delight in toying with gender stereotypes (she took great pleasure in the sexual ambiguity of her preferred nickname “Willie”), Barns-Graham ploughed her own furrow from the beginning. Born into an upper-class family in the seaside town of St Andrews in 1912, Barns-Graham’s resistance was tested early when her stern father became hostile towards her plan to pursue artmaking as a profession.

Nonetheless, ignited by her love of Cézanne, at the age of 18 Barns-Graham started studying at Edinburgh College of Art. “She had a single-mindedness,” Norris says. “She didn’t see any limitations, she just saw the path ahead.” It’s a focus you can sense in her 1945 oil painting Froth and Seaweed. Painted in her beloved St Ives, the artist homes in on the spidery tendrils of algae and slithery copper rock. “It’s almost as if she has no peripheral vision, she’s just seeing beauty at her feet.”

Film-maker Mark Cousins first encountered Barns-Graham’s paintings in late-80s Edinburgh. Whether depicting the silvery shorelines of St Ives and St Andrews or the crystalline glaciers of Switzerland, he says, “she just leapt off the walls”. He made a pilgrimage to her St Andrews house during lockdown, and in 2024 released A Sudden Glimpse to Deeper Things, which delves into the artist’s distinctive gaze and synesthesia. Barns-Graham associated colours with people, places, emotions and even letters of the alphabet – something she called a “total experience”. “If we think of Turner’s relationship to landscape, he saw a vortex. And Leonardo da Vinci saw a machine. She was like that as well; she saw a living thing,” Cousins says.

Her encounter with the Grindelwald glacier in Switzerland came in 1949. “That day was almost like a rebirth, a kind of rapture,” Cousins says of her life-defining hike and the 60-odd paintings and drawings that followed over a three-year period documenting the glacier’s “many moods”. In a letter to the Tate in 1965, she wrote: “It seemed to breathe!” This wasn’t an artist above the landscape, Norris says, but of the landscape. The glacier’s interiority was her interiority – a close symbiosis that intensified for the rest of her life as she pushed further into abstraction, moving away from figurative landscape painting in favour of “systems, rhythm, repetition and spatial tension”.

Yet the underlying presence of nature was still there: “bird flights, dancing diamonds on water, dots inside foxgloves, cell formations,” Norris writes. For the curator, Barns-Graham’s work in the 1960s-70s (titled Things of a Kind in Order and Disorder) is where she truly pioneered a new way of experiencing the world – “like chaos theory, really” – by laying out small cardboard squares in neat rows on her studio floor before randomly nudging them with her foot. On a stormy morning on the golden stretch of Porthmeor beach, I got to see this paint-splattered studio for myself; its floor-to-ceiling window looking out on to fast-moving clouds and ferocious waves.

Like Merce Cunningham’s “choreography by chance”, Barns-Graham was thinking about “how things hold together” – not least her marriage, which ended in divorce in 1963. Referring to her 1968 oil painting on board Olive Green Squares on Vermillion, she compared the erratic block of squares against a rage of red to “a broken marriage” – her own. Yet with Protest – another volatile blockwork which was made in 1967 as the Vietnam war raged and a year after the Beatles had released Revolver – “she was [also] thinking about participation and action and what you can do as an artist or viewer. She’s making the moves, she’s a part of it, she’s no longer in awe of a natural phenomenon that’s doing its own thing.”

When the Beatles came along, “working-class men were cool and posh women weren’t,” says Cousins. “But she just kept going.” In the 1980s, Barns-Graham’s tumult of squares made way for the thumbprint pen-and-ink lines of her Small Energy Drawings. “Are they soundwaves? Is it the wind?” Norris ponders. “Sometimes she’d look out from the cathedral-esque window of her studio in St Ives and turn her back to it, playing music and drawing lines that replicated the sea.” Another “choreography by chance”: first you observe, then you listen, then you feel. That precision and intuition can exist in such harmony in these artworks speaks profoundly to Barns-Graham’s own particular genius.

“At my age there’s no time to be lost,” Barns-Graham said in the 1990s. “I say to myself: ‘Do it now, say it now, don’t be afraid.’” Drawn to the late works of Picasso and Joan Miró, and incensed by the environmentally ruinous decade in which she was living (“the most appalling time of abuse of living things,” she remarked), the octogenarian slapped colour on to the canvas with an energy that was both urgent and physical. “The St Ives narrative flattened her,” Cousins says of this late flourish. “It saw her as one of many. It is important to extract her from St Ives and see her as a singular imaginative person.”
